strategy_title: Doubling num_warps at fixed XBLOCK doubles instruction count
strategy_description: Increasing num_warps from 4 to 8 at XBLOCK=128 doubled the block size from 128 to 256 threads, which doubled the executed instruction count (3.1M → 6.3M) and increased kernel duration from 8.26 µs to 13.66 µs (0.6x speedup). Although the No-Eligible scheduler stall rate improved modestly (34.87% → 27.95%) and L1 hit rate jumped dramatically (1% → 47.6%), the doubled instruction volume overwhelmed any latency-hiding benefit. In Triton, num_warps directly sets threads_per_block = num_warps × 32, so doubling num_warps at a fixed XBLOCK means each thread processes fewer elements but the block is twice as large, doubling total work dispatched per grid.
applicable_when: Never: this strategy caused regression. Avoid increasing num_warps beyond the natural XBLOCK/32 ratio in Triton pointwise kernels.
do_not_apply_when: When XBLOCK is fixed and num_warps > XBLOCK/32: in Triton, threads_per_block = num_warps × 32, so if num_warps × 32 > XBLOCK, each thread still processes exactly one element (XBLOCK elements / threads_per_block threads), but the block is larger, doubling total instructions dispatched. Do not apply when the kernel is already compute-bound (ALU >50%) and instruction count is the limiting factor. Do not apply when the scheduler No-Eligible rate is below 40% — the latency-hiding benefit is insufficient to offset the instruction volume increase.
framework_notes: Critical Triton semantics: in Triton, num_warps sets threads_per_block = num_warps × 32, independently of XBLOCK. When XBLOCK=128 and num_warps=8, threads_per_block=256 but only 128 elements are processed per block — each thread handles 0.5 elements on average, meaning half the threads are idle or the compiler unrolls differently. The autotuner selected num_warps=8 (block_size=256 in profiling), which doubled instruction count. In CUDA, the equivalent would be launching with 2× the threads per block while keeping the same work per block, which similarly wastes compute.

strategy_title: Precompute boundary masks to reduce redundant ALU ops
strategy_description: When a stencil or pooling kernel computes per-neighbor boundary masks by combining multiple boolean expressions redundantly (e.g., recomputing row/col validity for each of 9 neighbors independently), replacing them with 6 precomputed boundary boolean vectors (row_m1_ok, row_ok, row_p1_ok, col_m1_ok, col_ok, col_p1_ok) and reusing them across all loads reduces executed instruction count (3.1M → 2.7M) and warp cycles per issued instruction (18.3 → 15.9 cycles), yielding ~10% speedup. The reduction in ALU pressure also slightly increases effective memory throughput (456 → 505 GB/s) despite a small occupancy drop from increased register usage (22 → 26 regs/thread). This pattern is applicable whenever multiple loads share the same boundary condition logic that is currently recomputed per-load.
slow_pseudocode:
# Redundant mask recomputation per neighbor load
tmp0 = (-1) + x2; tmp2 = tmp0 >= 0; tmp4 = tmp0 < 14; tmp5 = tmp2 & tmp4  # row-1 valid
tmp6 = (-1) + x1; tmp7 = tmp6 >= 0; tmp8 = tmp6 < 14; tmp9 = tmp7 & tmp8  # col-1 valid
tmp10 = tmp5 & tmp9  # row-1 AND col-1
load0 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 7200, mask=tmp10 & xmask, other=-inf)
# ... repeat mask recomputation for each of 9 neighbors ...
tmp15 = x1 >= 0; tmp16 = x1 < 14; tmp17 = tmp15 & tmp16  # col valid (always true)
tmp18 = tmp5 & tmp17  # row-1 AND col
load1 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 6720, mask=tmp18 & xmask, other=-inf)
# ... 7 more loads with similar redundant boolean chains ...
fast_pseudocode:
# Precompute 4 boundary masks once, reuse across all 9 loads
row_m1_ok = x2 >= 1        # row-1 valid
row_p1_ok = x2 < 13        # row+1 valid
col_m1_ok = x1 >= 1        # col-1 valid
col_p1_ok = x1 < 13        # col+1 valid

tmp0 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 7200, mask=xmask & row_m1_ok & col_m1_ok, other=-inf)
tmp1 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 6720, mask=xmask & row_m1_ok,             other=-inf)
tmp2 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 6240, mask=xmask & row_m1_ok & col_p1_ok, other=-inf)
tmp3 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 480,  mask=xmask & col_m1_ok,             other=-inf)
tmp4 = tl.load(ptr + x6,        mask=xmask,                          other=-inf)
tmp5 = tl.load(ptr + x6 + 480,  mask=xmask & col_p1_ok,             other=-inf)
tmp6 = tl.load(ptr + x6 + 6240, mask=xmask & row_p1_ok & col_m1_ok, other=-inf)
tmp7 = tl.load(ptr + x6 + 6720, mask=xmask & row_p1_ok,             other=-inf)
tmp8 = tl.load(ptr + x6 + 7200, mask=xmask & row_p1_ok & col_p1_ok, other=-inf)

# Balanced tree reduction
result = tl.maximum(
    tl.maximum(tl.maximum(tmp0, tmp1), tl.maximum(tmp2, tmp3)),
    tl.maximum(tl.maximum(tmp4, tmp5), tl.maximum(tmp6, tl.maximum(tmp7, tmp8)))
)
applicable_when: Kernel performs a stencil or pooling operation with multiple neighbor loads sharing boundary conditions; profiling shows HighPipeUtilization (ALU >60%) with moderate warp cycles per issued instruction (>15); executed instruction count is high relative to the number of loads; boundary masks are recomputed independently per load rather than shared.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel is already memory-bound (memory throughput >70% of peak) rather than ALU-bound — reducing ALU ops will not help. Also avoid when the additional registers from precomputed mask variables would push register pressure high enough to significantly reduce block-limit-registers and occupancy (watch for >28 regs/thread with small block sizes).
framework_notes: In Triton, boolean mask vectors (e.g., x2 >= 1) are computed as per-element predicate vectors over the XBLOCK range. Combining them with & is cheap but recomputing the same sub-expression (e.g., row-1 validity) for each of 9 loads wastes ALU cycles. Precomputing once and reusing is equivalent to CSE (common subexpression elimination) that the compiler may not perform automatically across tl.load mask arguments.

strategy_title: Narrowing autotune configs to num_warps=8/16 forces large block size
strategy_description: Applying boundary mask hoisting and balanced tree reduction alongside a narrowed autotune config set (only XBLOCK=128 with num_warps=8/16/4) caused the autotuner to select num_warps=8, yielding block_size=256 — quadrupling executed instructions (1.78M → 5.47M) and increasing duration from 7.2 µs to 11.97 µs. The mask hoisting and tree reduction changes are semantically correct and beneficial in isolation (confirmed by exp_002_simplify_index_arithmetic_reduce_alu at +9.8%), but the regression was entirely caused by the autotune config change: removing the previously winning num_warps=2 config forced selection of a higher-warp config that inflated instruction count. When bundling kernel body improvements with autotune config changes, the config change can dominate and mask or reverse the body improvement.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE (winning config from iter 2): XBLOCK=128, num_warps=2, block_size=64, 7.2 µs
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=2),  # <-- this was selected
        # ... other configs ...
    ],
    key=['xnumel'],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    # hoisted masks + balanced tree (same body as after)
    row_m1_ok = x2 >= 1
    row_p1_ok = x2 < 13
    col_m1_ok = x1 >= 1
    col_p1_ok = x1 < 13
    v0 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 7200, mask=xmask & row_m1_ok & col_m1_ok, other=-inf)
    # ... 8 more loads ...
    result = tl.maximum(tl.maximum(a, b), tl.maximum(c, d))  # balanced tree
    tl.store(out_ptr + x6, result, xmask)
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER (regressed): XBLOCK=128, num_warps=8 selected, block_size=256, 11.97 µs
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=8,  num_stages=1),  # <-- selected
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=16, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=4,  num_stages=1),
        # num_warps=2 config REMOVED — this caused the regression
    ],
    key=['xnumel'],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(...):
    # same hoisted masks + balanced tree body
    row_m1_ok = x2 >= 1
    row_p1_ok = x2 < 13
    col_m1_ok = x1 >= 1
    col_p1_ok = x1 < 13
    v0 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 7200, mask=xmask & row_m1_ok & col_m1_ok, other=-inf)
    # ... 8 more loads ...
    result = tl.maximum(tl.maximum(a, b), tl.maximum(c, d))
    tl.store(out_ptr + x6, result, xmask)
applicable_when: Never apply this specific combination. The lesson is: when a previous iteration established a winning autotune config (e.g., num_warps=2), do not remove that config from the search space in subsequent iterations. Kernel body improvements should be applied while preserving the winning config set.
do_not_apply_when: Do not remove a previously winning autotune config (e.g., num_warps=2) when applying kernel body changes. Removing the winning config forces the autotuner to select a suboptimal config, which can dominate and reverse any body-level improvement. Specifically: do not narrow autotune configs to only high-num_warps options (≥4) for this kernel, as num_warps=8 at XBLOCK=128 produces block_size=256 and 3x more instructions than num_warps=2.
framework_notes: In Triton, the autotune config set is the primary lever controlling block_size (= num_warps × 32). When iterating on kernel body improvements, always include the previously winning config in the new autotune set. Adding num_stages=1 to configs is harmless for pointwise kernels (no pipelining benefit) but does not compensate for removing the winning num_warps value. The instruction count explosion (1.78M → 5.47M) at block_size=256 vs 64 is a 3.07× ratio, consistent with 4× more threads per block processing the same total elements with some overhead.

strategy_title: Simplify boundary mask expressions to reduce register pressure and instruction count
strategy_description: When a Triton stencil/pooling kernel already hoists boundary masks but uses compound boolean expressions (e.g., `(x2-1)>=0 & (x2-1)<14`), replacing them with simplified single-comparison forms (e.g., `x2>=1`) reduces both executed instruction count (1.78M→1.35M, -24%) and registers per thread (32→26), lowering warp cycles per issued instruction from 15.86 to 13.74 and yielding a 1.15x speedup. The autotune config set (XBLOCK=64, num_warps=2) was preserved from the prior winning iteration, so the block_size=64 configuration was maintained and the instruction reduction was the sole driver of improvement. This pattern applies whenever boundary mask boolean chains contain redundant sub-expressions that can be collapsed into a single comparison.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: compound mask expressions, 32 regs/thread, 1.78M instructions
row_m1 = ((x2 - 1) >= 0) & ((x2 - 1) < 14)  # two comparisons, redundant subtraction
row_p1 = ((x2 + 1) < 14)                      # one comparison
col_m1 = ((x1 - 1) >= 0) & ((x1 - 1) < 14)  # two comparisons, redundant subtraction
col_p1 = ((x1 + 1) < 14)                      # one comparison
v0 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 7200, mask=row_m1 & col_m1 & xmask, other=-inf)
# ... 8 more loads ...
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER: simplified single-comparison masks, 26 regs/thread, 1.35M instructions
row_m1_ok = x2 >= 1        # equiv to (x2-1)>=0 AND (x2-1)<14 since x2 in [0,13]
row_p1_ok = x2 < 13        # equiv to (x2+1)<14 since x2+1>=0 always
col_m1_ok = x1 >= 1        # equiv to (x1-1)>=0 AND (x1-1)<14 since x1 in [0,13]
col_p1_ok = x1 < 13        # equiv to (x1+1)<14 since x1+1>=0 always
v0 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 7200, mask=xmask & row_m1_ok & col_m1_ok, other=-inf)
# ... 8 more loads with simplified masks ...
applicable_when: Triton stencil/pooling kernel with hoisted boundary masks that still use compound boolean expressions (e.g., `(idx-1)>=0 & (idx-1)<N`) where the index range is statically bounded; profiling shows ALU pipeline utilization >30% and warp cycles per issued instruction >13; registers per thread are elevated (>28) suggesting compiler is materializing intermediate values for compound expressions.
do_not_apply_when: When the index range is not statically bounded and the compound expression is genuinely necessary for correctness (e.g., the index could be negative before the subtraction). Also avoid when register pressure is already low (<20 regs/thread) and the simplification would not reduce register count — the benefit is primarily from register reduction enabling better compiler optimization.
framework_notes: In Triton, boolean mask vectors are computed as per-element predicate vectors over the XBLOCK range. Compound expressions like `(x2-1)>=0 & (x2-1)<14` require the compiler to materialize `x2-1` as an intermediate vector and perform two comparisons, consuming extra registers. Simplifying to `x2>=1` (when x2 is known to be in [0,13]) eliminates the subtraction and one comparison, reducing both instruction count and register pressure. This is a form of strength reduction that the Triton compiler may not perform automatically.

strategy_title: Add XBLOCK=32/num_warps=1 config to unlock smaller block selection
strategy_description: Adding a smaller XBLOCK=32/num_warps=1 config to the autotune set for a latency-bound stencil kernel caused the autotuner to select it, halving executed instruction count (1.35M → 0.68M) and reducing warp cycles per issued instruction from 13.74 to 10.61 cycles, yielding a 1.17x speedup. Despite achieved occupancy dropping from 42.87% to 17.06% and No-Eligible stall rate worsening (47.77% → 71.69%), the reduced per-block instruction volume was sufficient to cut duration from 7.1 µs to 7.01 µs. The key constraint is that num_warps × 32 must equal XBLOCK to avoid idle threads: XBLOCK=32 with num_warps=1 gives exactly 32 threads/block, matching one warp per block.
applicable_when: Triton pointwise or stencil kernel where CPIStall is the dominant bottleneck; warp cycles per issued instruction >13; achieved occupancy is already low (<50%) and further occupancy reduction is acceptable; the current minimum XBLOCK config is ≥64 and no XBLOCK=32/num_warps=1 config exists in the autotune set; the grid uses a lambda so smaller XBLOCK configs correctly cover all elements.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel is memory-bandwidth-bound (DRAM throughput >60% of peak) — reducing block size reduces memory-level parallelism. Do not apply when achieved occupancy is already very low (<20%) and the bottleneck is latency hiding rather than instruction volume. Do not apply if num_warps × 32 ≠ XBLOCK for the new config, as this causes idle threads and instruction doubling. Do not apply if the grid is hardcoded to a fixed denominator rather than a lambda — the smaller XBLOCK would then fail to cover all elements.
framework_notes: In Triton, the constraint num_warps × 32 == XBLOCK ensures exactly one element per thread with no idle threads. For XBLOCK=32, num_warps=1 gives 32 threads/block = 1 warp/block. The grid must be a lambda `lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),)` so that smaller XBLOCK values correctly scale the grid size to cover all elements. A hardcoded grid denominator (e.g., `triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128)`) would under-cover elements when XBLOCK=32 is selected.

strategy_title: Add num_warps=1 config to further reduce CPI stalls
strategy_description: When a Triton pointwise/stencil kernel is dominated by CPIStall (L1TEX scoreboard stalls) and the prior winning config is already at num_warps=2 (block_size=64), adding a num_warps=1 config (block_size=32) to the autotune set can yield further speedup by reducing per-SM warp contention even further. In this case, warp cycles per issued instruction dropped from 13.74 to 8.91 (-35%) and executed instructions fell from 1.35M to 1.0M (-26%), producing a 1.15x speedup despite occupancy dropping from 42.9% to 19.2% and register pressure increasing from 26 to 36 regs/thread. The key insight is that for short-latency stencil kernels with low memory bandwidth utilization (<20% of peak), reducing warp count per block reduces scheduler contention more than it hurts latency hiding.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: autotune with 3 configs, winning = XBLOCK=64, num_warps=2 (block_size=64)
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 64},  num_warps=2, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=2, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 64},  num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
    ],
    key=['xnumel'],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(in_ptr0, out_ptr0, xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    row_m1_ok = x2 >= 1; row_p1_ok = x2 < 13
    col_m1_ok = x1 >= 1; col_p1_ok = x1 < 13
    tmp0 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 7200, mask=xmask & row_m1_ok & col_m1_ok, other=-inf, eviction_policy='evict_last')
    # ... 8 more loads ...
    result = tl.maximum(tl.maximum(tl.maximum(tmp0, tmp1), tl.maximum(tmp2, tmp3)),
                        tl.maximum(tl.maximum(tmp4, tmp5), tl.maximum(tmp6, tl.maximum(tmp7, tmp8))))
    tl.store(out_ptr + x6, result, xmask)
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER: 4 configs, new num_warps=1 added, winning = XBLOCK=64, num_warps=1 (block_size=32)
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 64},  num_warps=1, num_stages=1),  # <-- new, selected
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 64},  num_warps=2, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 128}, num_warps=2, num_stages=1),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 64},  num_warps=4, num_stages=1),
    ],
    key=['xnumel'],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(in_ptr0, out_ptr0, xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    row_m1_ok = x2 >= 1; row_p1_ok = x2 < 13
    col_m1_ok = x1 >= 1; col_p1_ok = x1 < 13
    tmp0 = tl.load(ptr + x6 - 7200, mask=xmask & row_m1_ok & col_m1_ok, other=-inf, eviction_policy='evict_last')
    # ... 8 more loads (identical body) ...
    result = tl.maximum(tl.maximum(tl.maximum(tmp0, tmp1), tl.maximum(tmp2, tmp3)),
                        tl.maximum(tl.maximum(tmp4, tmp5), tl.maximum(tmp6, tl.maximum(tmp7, tmp8))))
    tl.store(out_ptr + x6, result, xmask)
applicable_when: Triton pointwise or stencil kernel where CPIStall (L1TEX scoreboard) is the dominant bottleneck; current winning config is already at low num_warps (2); active warps per scheduler is moderate (5-10); memory bandwidth utilization is low (<20% of peak DRAM); kernel duration is short (<10 us) suggesting latency-bound rather than throughput-bound behavior. Adding num_warps=1 to the autotune config set is low-risk since the prior winning config is preserved.
do_not_apply_when: When the kernel is memory-bandwidth-bound (DRAM throughput >40% of peak) — reducing warps to 1 will eliminate memory-level parallelism and hurt bandwidth. Also avoid when achieved occupancy is already very low (<20%) and the bottleneck is latency hiding. Do not apply when register pressure at num_warps=1 would exceed the block limit registers threshold and reduce theoretical occupancy below 25% (check that registers_per_thread × 32 < SM register file size / max_blocks_per_SM). Note that num_warps=1 may increase register pressure (26→36 regs/thread here) due to compiler unrolling differently.
framework_notes: In Triton, num_warps=1 sets threads_per_block=32 (one warp per block). At XBLOCK=64 with num_warps=1, each thread processes 2 elements (XBLOCK/threads = 64/32 = 2), which the compiler handles via loop unrolling or vectorization. This increases register pressure (26→36 regs/thread) as the compiler materializes more intermediate values per thread. The key benefit is that with only 1 warp per block, scheduler contention is eliminated entirely within a block, and the CPIStall cycles drop dramatically (13.74→8.91 cycles/instruction). The grid size and waves_per_sm remain unchanged since grid = cdiv(xnumel, XBLOCK) is independent of num_warps.
